SH 288 serves as a major corridor connecting drivers from Brazoria and Harris Counties to areas like the Medical Center, Downtown Houston, and the Gulf Coast. checks.snippet: Skip to content TOLL ROADS ELECTRONIC TOLL TAG ONLY – NO CASH, NO PAY BY MAIL Click icon for more information Trip Building Process General Information Fort Bend Parkway Grand Parkway Westpark Tollway On February 18, 2018 Fort Bend County Toll Road Authority (FBCTRA) implemented a trip building process for toll tag transactions to reduce operational costs. A “trip” is defined as two (2) or more valid AVI (tag) transactions on a single roadway, in a single direction, within a maximum 4-hour time limit. For example, if you traveled the entire southbound length of Grand Parkway, currently you would see seven (7) $0.44 transactions on your toll tag statement. The trip building process would combine those seven (7) valid tag transactions into a single transaction showing as one (1) $3.08 transaction (7 x $0.44 = $3.08) on your toll tag statement. There is no additional cost or surcharge to the customer, just a new way to view the transactions on your toll tag statement. FBCTRA hosts a website WWW.MYFBCTRA.COM where you can view the individual transactions within each trip shown on your toll tag statement. Below is an example of the trip you will see on your statement – note that it will state ‘Trip End’ on the transaction if it is a trip (highlighted in below HCTRA example). You will use data found on your toll tag statement to login to WWW.MYFBCTRA.COM to view the individual transactions in the trip. The 10.3-mile project provides relief for those traveling between downtown Houston and Brazoria County, including connections to US 59/I-69, the Texas Medical Center, I-610 and Beltway 8 (Sam Houston Tollway). The toll lanes of the SH 288 Managed Lanes Project have a minimum target speed of 45 mph. For the SH 288 Managed Lanes Project to continue to offer a reliable commute, tolling prices are managed with the intent to provide predictable traffic conditions. Toll rates are based on the day of the week, time of day, number of axles, and historical utilization. Drivers on SH 288 managed lanes will incur toll charges at each mainline and direct connector toll gantry. All tolls are collected electronically, so there’s no stopping to pay at toll booths. Tolls are based on how far you drive and what kind of vehicle you're driving. Drivers pay a toll each time they pass through a toll plaza. Depending on where they get on or get off the road, drivers also pay a toll on certain entrance and exit ramps. Drivers without a toll tag pay 50 percent more on Austin-area toll roads. The two-axle tag and non-tag rates are rounded to the nearest cent. The remaining three or more axle rates are calculated using the two-axle rates multiplied by the N-1 formulas, where N is the number of axles. Additional fees apply for non‐tag transactions. Toll rates shown below are effective Jan. 1, 2026. For more information on toll rates, see Texas Transportation Commission records. checks.snippet: Skip to main content Careers Contact us English keyboard_arrow_down Discover Texas keyboard_arrow_down Data and maps keyboard_arrow_down Do business keyboard_arrow_down Explore projects keyboard_arrow_down Stay safe keyboard_arrow_down About keyboard_arrow_down Home Discover Texas Toll roads in Texas Discover Texas Toll roads in Texas Toll roads Managed lanes Paying tolls Programs TxTag/TxDOT does not send texts or emails for past due tolls. If you received an SMS text message or email regarding a past due or outstanding TxTag balance, it is a scam. Do not click on any links or provide any financial or personal information. Call 281-875-3279 to confirm if you have an outstanding toll balance. Toll roads in Texas 872 Miles of open toll facilities 225 Miles of future toll facilities 12 Toll road operators statewide 4 Toll tag operators Texas has more than a dozen toll operators across the state, each responsible for managing and maintaining their own toll roads. They include TxDOT, multiple toll road authorities and regional mobility authorities, and public-private partnerships (3Ps) with TxDOT. Although each entity sets its own business rules, billing practices and toll rates, all share a common goal: improving mobility for millions of motorists driving on Texas roads every day. Some operators issue their own toll tags, all of which are interoperable on toll roads in Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, Colorado and most of Florida.
